# Pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Internal medicine > Cardiology and angiology > Hypertensive disorders > Pulmonary hypertension and cor pulmonale*

[Original Article Link](/library/w50hmg)

---

## Summary

<u>Pulmonary hypertension</u> (<u>PH</u>) is defined by an elevated <u>mean pulmonary arterial pressure</u> (<u>mPAP</u>) > 20 mm Hg at rest. <u>PH</u> is divided into five groups based on the underlying causes: <u>pulmonary arterial hypertension</u> (<u>PAH</u>), left <u>heart</u> disease, chronic <u>lung</u> disease, <u>pulmonary artery</u> obstruction (e.g., due to chronic thromboembolic disease), and unclear multifactorial mechanisms. Over time, the increase in <u>right ventricular</u> pressure may result in structural changes (e.g., dilation or <u>hypertrophy</u>) or impaired function of the <u>right ventricle</u>, a cardiac condition known as <u>cor pulmonale</u>. While <u>PH</u> is often asymptomatic in the early stages, symptoms such as <u>dyspnea on exertion</u>, fatigue, <u>cyanosis</u>, and <u>syncope</u> appear in later stages. <u>Echocardiograms</u> are used as an initial noninvasive test to estimate <u>pulmonary artery</u> pressure and to evaluate for <u>right ventricular dysfunction</u>. <u>Right heart catheterization</u> provides a definite diagnosis by measuring <u>mPAP</u> but is not always required. Treatment mainly consists of managing the underlying <u>cause of PH</u> and preventing disease progression. Patients with <u>PAH</u> (i.e., <u>Group 1 PH</u>) usually benefit from treatment with <u>calcium channel blockers</u> and other <u>pulmonary vasodilators</u>, while their benefit is unclear for other groups. In most cases, evaluation by a <u>PH</u> specialist and referral to specialized centers is recommended. <u>Acute decompensated pulmonary hypertension</u> is a high-mortality complication that can occur and is very challenging to treat, typically requiring intensive care, and in some cases, <u>ECMO</u> and <u>lung transplant</u>. Some patients develop acute or chronic <u>cor pulmonale</u>, which requires treatment of the underlying cause and, in some cases, acute stabilization.




This article focuses primarily on adult <u>PH</u>. See “<u>Persistent pulmonary hypertension of the newborn</u> (<u>PPHN</u>)” for information on <u>PH</u> in <u>infants</u>.

---

## Definitions

* Pulmonary hypertension (<u>PH</u>) [[1]](/library/Z8YZOI)[[2]](/library/9tcNfV0)[[3]](/library/2FcThV0)

* An elevated <u>mean pulmonary arterial pressure</u> (<u>mPAP</u>) > 20 mm Hg at rest (normal: 10–14 mm Hg)  [[1]](/library/Z8YZOI)[[4]](/library/VKcG2W0)[[5]](/library/dycoVU0)[[6]](/library/VycGVU0)

* Subtypes

* Precapillary pulmonary hypertension

* Pulmonary vascular remodeling leads to increased <u>pulmonary vascular resistance</u>.

* Caused by <u>pulmonary arterial hypertension</u>, chronic <u>lung</u> disease, chronic <u>thromboembolism</u>, or certain multifactorial mechanisms

* <u>Right heart catheterization</u> shows increased <u>pulmonary vascular resistance</u> (≥ 3 <u>Wood units</u>) and reduced <u>pulmonary capillary wedge pressure</u> (<u>PCWP</u>).

* Postcapillary pulmonary hypertension

* Results from increased pulmonary venous pressure

* Caused by left <u>heart</u> disease and certain multifactorial mechanisms

* <u>Right heart catheterization</u> shows increased <u>PCWP</u>; <u>pulmonary vascular resistance</u> is typically normal.

* Pulmonary arterial hypertension (<u>PAH</u>): a type of <u>precapillary pulmonary hypertension</u> characterized by loss and obstructive remodeling of the pulmonary vascular bed that results in increased pulmonary arterial pressure (See “Etiology” for underlying causes) [[7]](/library/TLc6C10)





> [!TIP]
> <u>Pulmonary arterial hypertension</u> is a <u>cause of pulmonary hypertension</u>. However, not all <u>pulmonary hypertension</u> is caused by <u>pulmonary arterial hypertension</u>.

---

## Epidemiology

* <u>PAH</u>: more commonly affects female individuals



Epidemiological data refers to the US, unless otherwise specified.

---

## Etiology

The following etiologies are grouped according to the <u>World Health Organization</u> (WHO) classification system for <u>pulmonary hypertension</u>. [[7]](/library/TLc6C10)[[8]](/library/YycndU0)[[9]](/library/cycaVU0)




### <u>Pulmonary arterial hypertension</u> (Group 1 PH)




* <u>Idiopathic</u>

* Hereditary (e.g., <u>BMPR2</u> <u>loss-of-function</u> mutation)

* Encodes a set of inhibitors of vascular <u>smooth muscle cell</u> <u>proliferation</u>

* Associated with a poor prognosis

* Drug-induced [[8]](/library/YycndU0)

* <u>Methamphetamine</u> (and possibly <u>amphetamines</u> and <u>cocaine</u>)

* <u>Sympathomimetic</u> appetite suppressants (e.g., <u>diethylpropion</u>, fenfluramine)

* <u>Chemotherapeutic agents</u>, e.g., <u>dasatinib</u>

* Associated conditions

* <u>Connective tissue diseases</u>, e.g., <u>systemic sclerosis</u>

* <u>Portopulmonary hypertension</u>

* <u>Congenital heart disease</u> (e.g., <u>left-to-right shunt</u>, <u>Eisenmenger syndrome</u>)

* <u>HIV infection</u>

* <u>Schistosomiasis</u>

* <u>PPHN</u>





### Left <u>heart</u> disease (Group 2 PH)




* <u>Congestive heart failure</u> (<u>CHF</u>): e.g., <u>HFrEF</u>, <u>HFpEF</u>

* <u>Valvular heart diseases</u>, e.g., <u>aortic valve stenosis</u>, <u>mitral valve stenosis</u>

* Other acquired or <u>congenital heart diseases</u> causing <u>postcapillary PH</u> (e.g., <u>hypoplastic left heart</u>, <u>aortic coarctation</u>, <u>HCM</u>, <u>LVOT obstruction</u>)





### Chronic <u>lung</u> diseases (Group 3 PH)




* <u>Obstructive lung diseases</u>

* <u>COPD</u>, <u>emphysema</u>

* <u>Obstructive sleep apnea</u>

* <u>Restrictive lung diseases</u>: e.g., <u>interstitial lung disease</u>

* High altitude (e.g., high-altitude <u>pulmonary hypertension</u>)

* Others: e.g., developmental <u>lung</u> disorders, mixed obstructive and <u>restrictive lung diseases</u>





### <u>Pulmonary artery</u> obstruction (Group 4 PH) [[8]](/library/YycndU0)




* Chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension (<u>CTEPH</u>): Chronic thromboembolic occlusion of the pulmonary vessels

* Recurrent microthrombi narrow the cross-sectional area of pulmonary vessels.

* Affected individuals are at high risk for <u>pulmonary embolism</u>.

* Other causes of <u>pulmonary artery</u> (PA) obstruction: extrinsic compression by <u>mediastinal</u> tumors or masses, arteritis involving PAs, congenital PA stenoses, <u>fibrosing mediastinitis</u> [[10]](/library/nyc7fU0)





### Unclear multifactorial mechanisms (Group 5 PH)




* Hematologic disorders (e.g., <u>sickle cell disease</u>, <u>MPNs</u>, chronic <u>hemolytic anemias</u>)

* Systemic disorders (e.g., <u>sarcoidosis</u>, <u>neurofibromatosis</u>, <u>Langerhans cell histiocytosis</u>)

* Metabolic disorders (e.g., <u>metabolic syndrome</u>, <u>chronic kidney disease</u>, <u>Gaucher disease</u>)

* Complex <u>congenital heart disease</u>  [[11]](/library/Xyc9dU0)





### Conditions at high risk of PH [[12]](/library/hFcc3V0)




Periodic screening and monitoring for clinical <u>features of PH</u> is suggested for patients with any of the following:




* <u>Family history</u> of <u>PAH</u>

* Genetic screening positive in the patient or 1st-degree relative (e.g., for <u>BMPR2</u>)

* Exposure to drug or toxin known to cause <u>PH</u> (e.g., <u>methamphetamine</u>, fenfluramine)

* <u>Scleroderma</u>

* <u>Mixed connective tissue diseases</u>

* <u>HIV</u>

* <u>Portal hypertension</u>

* Recent (e.g., within the last 3–6 months) surgical repair of a congenital <u>left-to-right shunt</u>

---

## Pathophysiology

* Increased <u>pulmonary vascular resistance</u>

* Occlusive vasculopathy (e.g., <u>idiopathic</u> <u>pulmonary arterial hypertension</u>, <u>connective tissue diseases</u>)

* <u>Hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction</u>: chronic <u>hypoxic</u> pulmonary <u>vasoconstriction</u> → <u>airway</u> <u>smooth muscle</u> <u>hypertrophy</u> (<u>medial</u> <u>hypertrophy</u>) and pulmonary vascular bed destruction → ↑ <u>pulmonary vascular resistance</u> (e.g., <u>COPD</u>, <u>obstructive sleep apnea</u>)

* Increased pulmonary vessel pressure → right <u>heart</u> <u>hypertrophy</u> → <u>right heart failure</u> (<u>cor pulmonale</u>) and <u>arrhythmias</u> → <u>death</u>

* Inflammation (e.g., <u>COPD</u>) → ↑ inflammatory cell infiltration of <u>intima</u> → thickened <u>endothelial</u> wall → <u>intimal</u> <u>fibrosis</u>

* <u>PAH</u> associated with <u>endothelial</u> dysfunction: ↑ <u>endothelin</u> and ↓ <u>vasodilators</u> (e.g., NO, <u>prostacyclins</u>) → <u>vasoconstriction</u> → <u>arteriosclerosis</u>, plexiform lesions [[13]](/library/BOYzu6)

* Increased pulmonary venous pressure: volume or pressure overload from left-sided <u>heart</u> disease (e.g. <u>mitral valve regurgitation</u>)

* Increased pulmonary blood flow

* <u>Left-to-right shunt</u> (e.g., <u>ASD</u>, <u>VSD</u>, <u>PDA</u>)

* <u>Portopulmonary hypertension</u>

* <u>Sickle cell anemia</u>: Individuals with <u>SCD</u> have an <u>anemia</u>-induced increase in <u>cardiac output</u>.





> [!NOTE]
> Increased pressure in pulmonary circuit → ↑ right ventricular <u>afterload</u> → dilatation and/or <u>hypertrophy</u> of the right <u>heart</u> → <u>right heart failure</u> and <u>arrhythmias</u> → <u>death</u>.

---

## Clinical features

Patients with early <u>PH</u> may be asymptomatic.




* Common clinical features

* <u>Dyspnea</u> and/or <u>syncope</u> on exertion

* <u>Chest pain</u>

* Fatigue

* <u>Cyanosis</u>

* Clinical features of underlying etiology (e.g., <u>COPD</u>, <u>OSA</u>, <u>PE</u>)

* Less common clinical features

* <u>Hoarseness</u>

* <u>Cough</u>, <u>hemoptysis</u>

* <u>Physical examination</u> 

* Loud and palpable <u>second heart sound</u> (often split)

* <u>Jugular vein distention</u>

* <u>Symptoms of right heart failure</u> (e.g., <u>palpitations</u>, <u>peripheral edema</u>, <u>hepatojugular reflux</u>)

* <u>Nail clubbing</u>

* <u>Parasternal heave</u>





![Digital clubbing](media/can84kn62cgi6f4l0bc3p1f3.jpg)

Digital clubbing




> [!TIP]
> Clinical symptoms may be inconspicuous, especially in the early stages when symptoms of underlying diseases such as <u>COPD</u> may eclipse those of <u>PH</u>.

---

## Diagnosis

### Approach [[4]](/library/VKcG2W0)[[14]](/library/nyb7fw)




Due to overlapping clinical features, <u>PH</u> is often diagnosed during the evaluation of more common differential diagnoses and etiologies of <u>dyspnea</u>, <u>chest pain</u>, and fatigue (e.g., <u>COPD</u>, <u>CHF</u>, <u>cardiomyopathy</u>, <u>PE</u>, <u>OSA</u>), or identified during screening <u>echocardiography</u> or <u>cardiac catheterization</u> (e.g., <u>preoperative assessment</u>).




* Screen and monitor patients with <u>conditions at high risk of PH</u> for suggestive clinical features. [[12]](/library/hFcc3V0)

* If clinical suspicion is high for <u>PH</u>, perform <u>transthoracic echocardiography</u> (<u>TTE</u>) to noninvasively identify markers of elevated <u>pulmonary artery</u> pressure.

* If <u>TTE</u> suggests <u>PH</u> and the etiology is not yet known, begin evaluation for the most common underlying causes.

* Identify clinical evidence of left <u>heart</u> disease and/or chronic <u>lung</u> disease and consider supportive investigations (e.g., <u>ECG</u>, <u>CXR</u>, <u>BNP</u>, <u>PFTs</u>) as directed by clinical suspicion.

* If these are inconclusive, perform a <u>V/Q scan</u> to evaluate for thromboembolic disease.

* If the etiology remains unclear, <u>TTE</u> is equivocal, and/or severe <u>PH</u> is identified (see “Severity assessment”):

* Consult a <u>PH</u> specialist.

* Refer for confirmatory <u>right heart catheterization</u>.

* Consider more advanced investigations, e.g., genetic screening.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Right heart catheterization</u> can typically be deferred if <u>echocardiography</u> strongly suggests <u>PH</u>, the underlying etiology is clear (e.g., <u>COPD</u>), and the disease is nonsevere.




> [!TIP]
> <u>CXR</u>, <u>ECG</u>, and <u>laboratory studies</u> are not required to diagnose <u>pulmonary hypertension</u>, but they may support the diagnosis and help identify the underlying etiology.




### <u>Transthoracic echocardiography</u> (<u>TTE</u>) [[4]](/library/VKcG2W0)[[7]](/library/TLc6C10)




For clinical purposes, noninvasive estimates of <u>mPAP</u> and its <u>surrogate</u> markers, <u>pulmonary artery systolic pressure</u> (<u>PASP</u>) and <u>right ventricular</u> systolic pressure (RVSP), are typically accurate enough to make a diagnosis of <u>PH</u> and guide therapy. [[15]](/library/5ycifU0)




* Indication: : first-line study in all patients with suspected <u>PH</u> [[7]](/library/TLc6C10)

* Findings: A combination of findings can be used to estimate <u>PASP</u>, RVSP, and <u>mPAP</u>.   [[16]](/library/lycv2U0)[[17]](/library/Nyc-2U0)

* ↑ Tricuspid <u>regurgitation</u> <u>velocity</u> (<u>TRV</u>)

* <u>Right ventricular</u> pressure overload  

* Flattening of the interventricular septum

* <u>Hypertrophy</u> of the <u>right ventricle</u>

* Dilation of the <u>coronary sinus</u>  [[18]](/library/ijYJZ6)[[19]](/library/OycI2U0)

* <u>Right ventricular failure</u>

* Dilation and hypokinesis of the <u>right ventricle</u>

* Right atrial dilation

* Underfilled left <u>heart chambers</u>

* Evidence of underlying cardiovascular disease

* <u>Left ventricular dysfunction</u>

* <u>Mitral regurgitation</u>

* <u>Mitral stenosis</u>

* <u>Thrombus</u> in the right <u>heart</u>, <u>pulmonary artery</u>, or <u>IVC</u>





![Echocardiogram in pulmonary artery hypertension (1/3)](media/fay4fpxilz8fvdtropq0vzmy.jpg)

Echocardiogram in pulmonary artery hypertension (1/3)

![Echocardiogram in pulmonary artery hypertension (2/3)](media/y2841tgfo9yrig2ygnzmmurv.jpg)

Echocardiogram in pulmonary artery hypertension (2/3)

![Echocardiogram in pulmonary artery hypertension (3/3)](media/hb82esdbkgolrlkltj7480s3.jpg)

Echocardiogram in pulmonary artery hypertension (3/3)

![Right atrial thrombus](media/h3fw06ec44n7pra6l8hdkvlb.jpg)

Right atrial thrombus




> [!TIP]
> <u>Echocardiography</u> can also be used to screen patients at high risk for early <u>features of pulmonary hypertension</u>.




### <u>Right heart catheterization</u> [[1]](/library/Z8YZOI)[[4]](/library/VKcG2W0)




Obtain <u>right heart catheterization</u> in consultation with a <u>PH</u> specialist to ensure that individual patient-specific questions are addressed.




* Indications

* <u>Confirmatory test</u> for <u>pulmonary hypertension</u>

* Detailed assessment of other cardiac diseases (e.g., <u>valvular heart disease</u>, <u>coronary artery disease</u>)

* Findings: <u>mPAP</u> > 20 mm Hg at rest is considered diagnostic for <u>PH</u>.  [[1]](/library/Z8YZOI)[[4]](/library/VKcG2W0)

* <u>Precapillary pulmonary hypertension</u>, e.g., <u>PAH</u>

* <u>Pulmonary vascular resistance</u> ≥ 3 <u>Wood units</u> (normal: 0.25–1.6 <u>Wood units</u>)

* <u>PCWP</u> ≤ 15 mm Hg

* <u>Postcapillary pulmonary hypertension</u> and mixed pre- and <u>postcapillary pulmonary hypertension</u>, e.g., secondary to left <u>heart</u> disease

* <u>Pulmonary vascular resistance</u> is variable.

* <u>PCWP</u> > 15 mm Hg





### <u>ECG</u> [[20]](/library/UocbYW0)




* Typically shows nonspecific changes secondary to increased <u>right ventricular</u> workload 

* <u>Right ventricular hypertrophy</u>

* <u>Right-axis deviation</u>

* <u>P pulmonale</u>

* Incomplete or complete <u>right bundle branch block</u>

* <u>S1Q3T3</u>

* May also show signs of underlying etiology, e.g., <u>ischemic heart disease</u>





![ECG in pulmonary hypertension secondary to an atrial septal defect](media/tj1laprl07rgvc4wn6intawy.jpg)

ECG in pulmonary hypertension secondary to an atrial septal defect

![Right ventricular hypertrophy with extreme right-axis deviation](media/vgsecqsub1i03ee60tojexft.jpg)

Right ventricular hypertrophy with extreme right-axis deviation




### <u>Chest x-ray</u> [[14]](/library/nyb7fw)[[21]](/library/gocFYW0)




<u>Chest x-ray</u> findings may help to support the diagnosis of <u>PH</u>.  [[21]](/library/gocFYW0)




* Right <u>heart</u> <u>hypertrophy</u> 

* Prominent right <u>heart</u> border

* <u>Lateral</u> view: loss of retrosternal space due to <u>right ventricular</u> enlargement

* Vascular changes

* Enlarged central <u>pulmonary arteries</u>

* Reduction in number and size of vessels of the peripheral pulmonary vasculature (referred to as pulmonary vascular pruning)

* Signs of the underlying cause (e.g., nodular opacities in <u>interstitial lung disease</u>, hyperinflation in <u>COPD</u>, pulmonary venous congestion in left <u>heart</u> disease)





![Pulmonary hypertension (1/2)](media/faavxvpvah72ihruf0vvumqr.jpg)

Pulmonary hypertension (1/2)

![Pulmonary hypertension (2/2)](media/gfhxhefiu7c405uhpmhnlo9t.jpg)

Pulmonary hypertension (2/2)




### Investigations of the underlying cause




Consider adding the following based on clinical suspicion of the underlying etiology:




* Left <u>heart</u> disease: <u>NT-proBNP</u> (See also “Diagnosis” in “<u>CHF</u>” and “<u>Mitral regurgitation</u>.”)

* Chronic <u>lung</u> disease (See also "Diagnosis" in “<u>COPD</u>,” “<u>ILD</u>,” and “<u>OSA</u>.”)

* <u>Arterial blood gas</u>

* <u>Pulmonary function tests</u>

* <u>Diffusion capacity for carbon monoxide</u>

* Consider CT chest and <u>sleep studies</u>.

* Chronic <u>pulmonary thromboembolism</u>: <u>V/Q scan</u> (See also “ <u>PE diagnostics</u>.”)

* Others: Consider if etiology remains unclear after investigations for left-<u>heart</u> disease, chronic <u>lung</u> disease, and <u>CTEPH</u>. [[22]](/library/kIYm1q)

* Drug-induced: e.g., <u>urine drug screen</u>

* <u>Portopulmonary hypertension</u>: Send <u>liver chemistries</u>, consider <u>ultrasound</u> <u>liver</u>.

* Infection (based on <u>risk factors</u>): e.g., <u>screen for HIV</u> and <u>schistosomiasis</u>.

* <u>Connective tissue disease</u> (most commonly <u>systemic sclerosis</u>): e.g., <u>antinuclear antibodies</u>, <u>anticentromere antibodies</u>, <u>anti-Scl-70</u> and <u>anti-RNA polymerase III</u>

* <u>Sarcoidosis</u>: e.g., <u>inflammatory markers</u>, serum <u>calcium</u>, <u>ACE</u> levels

* Hereditary: e.g., <u>genetic testing</u>





> [!TIP]
> If <u>PH</u> is not explained by left <u>heart</u> disease or chronic <u>lung</u> disease, perform a <u>V/Q scan</u> to exclude <u>CTEPH</u>. [[7]](/library/TLc6C10)




![Mismatched perfusion defects from pulmonary emboli](media/s2o0w0bcr277dpy2wvpo20m0.jpg)

Mismatched perfusion defects from pulmonary emboli

---

## Treatment

### Approach




* Treat <u>acute decompensated PH</u> urgently, if present.

* Determine functional severity and screen for high-risk features; consult <u>PAH</u> specialist and strongly consider admission to <u>PAH</u> specialty center if present.

* Tailor treatment according to <u>WHO PH group</u> (see “Long-term management”).

* Start supportive treatment to reduce symptoms and slow progression.

* Consider directed therapies for Group I <u>PH</u> (i.e., <u>PAH</u>): e.g., <u>CCBs</u> and/or other <u>pulmonary vasodilators</u>.

* Treat the underlying <u>cause of PH</u> (e.g., <u>CPAP</u> for patients with <u>OSA</u>, <u>CHF treatment</u>, <u>anticoagulation for PE</u>).





> [!TIP]
> Therapy should be initiated early before irreversible changes in the pulmonary vessels occur.




> [!WARNING]
> <u>Pulmonary vasodilators</u> are not typically beneficial for patients with <u>Group 2 PH</u> (left <u>heart</u> disease) or <u>Group 3 PH</u> (chronic <u>lung</u> disease).




### Severity assessment




#### WHO functional class for PH (<u>WHO-FC</u>) [[23]](/library/fyckeU0)




The <u>WHO-FC</u> system for <u>pulmonary hypertension</u> is widely used to help guide therapy.  [[12]](/library/hFcc3V0)[[24]](/library/a7cQ4d0)




* <u>WHO-FC</u> I: No limitations in physical activity; no significant symptoms during most regular <u>ADLs</u> and <u>IADLs</u>

* <u>WHO-FC</u> II: Slightly limited physical activity; no rest symptoms, but some symptoms during <u>IADLs</u>

* <u>WHO-FC</u> III: Noticeably limited physical activity; consistent symptoms during <u>basic ADLs</u>

* <u>WHO-FC</u> IV: Severely limited physical activity; frequent and/or progressive symptoms with almost any activity or even at rest





#### High-risk features [[24]](/library/a7cQ4d0)




The presence of any of the following features typically warrants admission to a <u>PAH</u> specialty center for evaluation and treatment. Stabilization in an <u>ICU</u> setting may be required in some cases.




* Rapidly progressing symptoms

* Unclear <u>PH</u> etiology

* Thromboembolic disease

* Severe <u>PH</u> (e.g., <u>WHO-FC</u> III-IV)

* Significantly elevated <u>NT-proBNP</u>

* RV dysfunction

---

## Long-term management

Consider individualized treatment based on the underlying condition and patient characteristics under the guidance of an appropriate specialist (e.g., cardiology, pulmonology). <u>Calcium channel blockers</u> and other <u>pulmonary vasodilators</u> are the mainstay of treatment for Group I <u>PH</u> (i.e., <u>PAH</u>), while treatment of the underlying cause is the primary focus for the other <u>WHO PH groups</u>.




### <u>Supportive care</u> [[24]](/library/a7cQ4d0)[[30]](/library/AtcRTV0)[[31]](/library/ZFcZgV0)




* <u>Oxygen therapy</u> for patients with <u>COPD</u> and a <u>PaO<sub>2</sub></u>< 60 mm Hg

* <u>Diuretics</u> for <u>volume overload</u>

* Immunizations

* Psychosocial support

* Exercise training  [[32]](/library/BtczfV0)

* Avoidance of the following, whenever possible: [[12]](/library/hFcc3V0)

* <u>Pregnancy</u>: Offer <u>counseling on contraception options</u>.; see “<u>PH and pregnancy</u>” for details.  [[4]](/library/VKcG2W0)[[33]](/library/f4Xkiy)

* High altitude

* Nonessential surgeries

* Consider referral to <u>palliative care</u> for patients with advanced <u>PH</u> and distressing symptoms.





> [!WARNING]
> Overdiuresis may reduce <u>right ventricular</u> <u>preload</u>, resulting in decreased <u>cardiac output</u> and subsequent complications, e.g., <u>prerenal failure</u>.




> [!TIP]
> Patients who have a normal <u>oxygen saturation</u> at rest may desaturate with exercise or while sleeping; perform exercise and nocturnal oximetry and treat accordingly.




### <u>Group 1 PH</u>: <u>PAH</u> [[12]](/library/hFcc3V0)[[34]](/library/Y7cn4d0)




Refer all patients to a specialist <u>PAH</u> center for assessment and <u>vasoreactivity testing</u> prior to starting pulmonary <u>vasodilator</u> therapy aimed at decreasing <u>pulmonary vascular resistance</u>.




* Vasoreactivity testing: A test performed during <u>right heart catheterization</u> to identify responsiveness to <u>calcium channel blocker</u> (<u>CCB</u>) therapy; <u>mPAP</u> is measured after administration of a <u>vasodilator</u> (e.g., <u>inhaled nitric oxide</u>)  [[34]](/library/Y7cn4d0)

* Vasoreactive:  Treat with <u>CCBs</u>.

* Nonvasoreactive: Consider other pulmonary <u>vasodilator</u> therapies.

* <u>Calcium channel blockers</u>: First-line pulmonary <u>vasodilator</u> therapy for patients with <u>PAH</u> and positive <u>vasoreactivity testing</u> and no <u>signs of RHF</u> or other contraindications to <u>CCBs</u>  [[12]](/library/hFcc3V0)

* Other pulmonary <u>vasodilator</u> therapies: typically second-line agents, the choice of which depends on symptom severity (e.g., <u>WHO-FC</u>) and should be guided by a <u>PAH</u> specialist. [[7]](/library/TLc6C10)[[12]](/library/hFcc3V0)

* Most patients (e.g., <u>WHO-FC</u> II-III) receive initial combination oral therapy (e.g., <u>PDE-5 inhibitor</u> PLUS <u>endothelin receptor antagonist</u>).

* Most high-risk patients (e.g., <u>WHO-FC</u> III-IV or rapidly progressive disease) are treated with parenteral <u>prostacyclins</u> (either as first-line or in combination)





| Overview of specific pulmonary vasodilator agents |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
| --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Agents |  | Clinical applications |  | Mechanism of action | Adverse effects | Contraindications | Interactions |  |
| <br>Endothelin receptor antagonists (e.g., bosentan, macitentan, <u>ambrisentan</u>) [[35]](/library/Udcb6Y0)<br> |  | <br>* <u>Pulmonary hypertension</u><br><br> |  | <br>* <u>Competitively inhibit</u> <u>endothelin-1</u> <u>receptors</u> → ↓ <u>vasoconstriction</u> in the pulmonary circuit<br><br> | <br>* <u>Hepatotoxicity</u>: <u>Liver function</u> tests should be monitored.<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Pregnancy</u><br><br>* Concomitant <u>cyclosporine</u> and <u>glyburide</u> use<br><br>* Hypersensitivity<br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Hormonal contraceptives</u>: ↓ <u>effectiveness</u><br><br> |  |
| <br><u>Phosphodiesterase-5 inhibitors</u> (e.g., <u>sildenafil</u>) |  | <br><br>* <u>Pulmonary hypertension</u><br><br>* <u>Erectile dysfunction</u><br><br><br> |  | <br>* PDE5 inhibition → ↓ breakdown of <u>cGMP</u> → pulmonary <u>vasodilation</u>, penile <u>smooth muscle</u> relaxation, and ↑ blood flow<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Headaches</u>, cutaneous flushing<br><br>* <u>Lightheadedness</u><br><br>* Visual deficits (blue-tinted <u>vision</u>; cyanopsia)<br><br><br> | <br>* Use of <u>alpha blockers</u> and <u>nitrates</u>: life-threatening <u>hypotension</u><br><br> |  |  |
| <br><u>Prostacyclin analogs</u> (<u>iloprost</u>, treprostinil) |  | <br><br>* <u>Pulmonary hypertension</u><br><br>* <u>Chronic limb-threatening ischemia</u><br><br><br> |  | <br><br>* <u>Prostacyclin</u> (<u>PGI<sub>2</sub></u>) acts as a direct <u>vasodilator</u> (systemic and pulmonary) and inhibits <u>platelet aggregation</u> via <u>prostacyclin</u> <u>receptors</u>.<br><br>* <u>Receptor</u> binding of <u>prostacyclins</u> or <u>prostacyclin analogs</u> → ↑ intracellular <u>cAMP</u> → inhibition of <u>myosin light chain kinase</u> → vascular <u>smooth muscle</u> relaxation<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Jaw</u> <u>pain</u><br><br>* Facial or generalized flushing<br><br><br> | <br>* None [[36]](/library/2dcT6Y0)<br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Anticoagulants</u>: ↑ risk of bleeding<br><br>* <u>Antihypertensives</u>, <u>vasodilators</u>: <u>hypotension</u><br><br><br> |  |
| <br>Synthetic <u>prostacyclin</u> (<u>epoprostenol</u>) [[37]](/library/fdck6Y0)<br> |  | <br><br>* <u>Heart failure with reduced ejection fraction</u><br><br>* Hypersensitivity<br><br><br> |  |  |  |  |  |  |




* Surgical therapy for refractory <u>PAH</u>

* Atrial septostomy (<u>right-to-left shunt</u>)

* <u>Heart</u>-<u>lung</u>/bilateral <u>lung transplantation</u>  [[38]](/library/wochVW0)[[39]](/library/jFc_3V0)




### <u>Group 2 PH</u>: Left-sided <u>heart</u> disease [[7]](/library/TLc6C10)[[14]](/library/nyb7fw)




* Treat systemic <u>hypertension</u> (see “<u>Hypertension management</u>”).

* Provide <u>CHF treatment</u> as needed.

* Consider <u>diuretics</u> to manage <u>volume overload</u>.

* Restrict <u>sodium</u> intake.

* Consider replacement or repair of damaged valves (see “<u>Aortic valve stenosis</u>”, “<u>Aortic regurgitation</u>, “<u>Mitral valve stenosis</u>”, and “<u>Mitral regurgitation</u>”).

* Aggressively treat any <u>atrial fibrillation</u> (see “<u>Management of Afib with RVR</u>” and “<u>Management of Afib in CHF</u>”).

* Treat comorbidities, e.g., <u>diabetes</u>, <u>obesity</u>, <u>management of ASCVD</u>.





### <u>Group 3 PH</u>: Chronic <u>lung</u> disease [[7]](/library/TLc6C10)[[14]](/library/nyb7fw)




* Start <u>long-term oxygen therapy</u>.

* Optimize treatment of underlying <u>COPD</u> or <u>interstitial lung disease</u>.

* Consider <u>lung transplantation</u>.





### <u>Group 4 PH</u>: PA obstruction




* <u>CTEPH</u> [[40]](/library/O7cINd0)

* <u>Pulmonary endarterectomy</u> is the first-line treatment.

* Consider balloon pulmonary <u>angioplasty</u> if the patient is ineligible for <u>pulmonary endarterectomy</u> or if <u>PH</u> persists or recurs.

* Consider certain <u>pulmonary vasodilators</u> in select cases.

* Treat associated <u>hypoxia</u> and <u>heart failure</u>.

* Lifelong anticoagulation

* Extrinsic compression (rare): Consider treatment tailored to the individual extrinsic etiology. [[10]](/library/nyc7fU0)





### <u>Group 5 PH</u>: <u>Multifactorial diseases</u> [[41]](/library/j7c_ld0)




* Direct initial therapy at the underlying <u>cause of PH</u>.

* Consider pulmonary <u>vasodilator</u> therapy on a case-by-case basis.

## Cor pulmonale

### Definition [[42]](/library/RFcl3V0)




Altered structure (i.e., <u>hypertrophy</u>, dilation) or impaired function of the <u>right ventricle</u> due to <u>pulmonary hypertension</u> resulting from a primary disorder of the respiratory or <u>pulmonary artery</u> system




> [!TIP]
> <u>Cor pulmonale</u> is also known as <u>pulmonary heart disease</u> because it is caused by <u>right ventricular dysfunction</u> resulting from <u>lung</u> disease, not cardiac disease. [[22]](/library/kIYm1q)




### Acute <u>cor pulmonale</u> [[22]](/library/kIYm1q)




* Pathophysiology: a sudden increase in <u>right ventricular</u> <u>afterload</u> results in <u>right ventricular</u> dilation and dysfunction

* Etiology: : includes acute <u>massive pulmonary embolism</u> (most common) and <u>ARDS</u>  [[43]](/library/iFcJ3V0)

* Clinical features: acute onset, <u>chest pain</u>, <u>shortness of breath</u>, <u>hypotension</u>, <u>tachycardia</u>, <u>syncope</u>, symptoms of <u>deep vein thrombosis</u>





![Acute and chronic pulmonary emboli](media/jm0rh9oabemfx8d42gq0zlzh.jpg)

Acute and chronic pulmonary emboli




### Chronic <u>cor pulmonale</u> [[22]](/library/kIYm1q)




* Pathophysiology: Increased <u>right ventricular</u> <u>afterload</u> leads to progressive <u>right ventricular hypertrophy</u> that over time results in <u>right ventricular</u> dilation and dysfunction.

* Etiology: caused by diseases of the <u>lung parenchyma</u> and pulmonary vasculature or disorders of chronic <u>hypoxia</u>

* <u>Lung parenchyma</u>: <u>COPD</u> , <u>interstitial lung disease</u>, <u>bronchiectasis</u>

* Pulmonary vasculature: <u>PAH</u>, <u>chronic thromboembolic pulmonary hypertension</u>

* Chronic <u>hypoxia</u>: <u>obesity hypoventilation syndrome</u>, <u>obstructive sleep apnea</u>, <u>kyphoscoliosis</u>, neuromuscular disorders

* Clinical features

* Similar to <u>clinical features of pulmonary hypertension</u>.

* Prominent <u>symptoms of right heart failure</u>





### Diagnostics [[42]](/library/RFcl3V0)




* <u>Echocardiogram</u> shows <u>right ventricular</u> dilation, <u>hypertrophy</u>, or dysfunction.

* Further workup depends on the suspected underlying cause; see “Diagnostics” of “<u>Pulmonary hypertension</u>.”

* For patients with suspected acute <u>cor pulmonale</u>, urgently perform <u>diagnostic studies for PE</u>.





### Treatment




* Treatment depends on the underlying cause (see “<u>Treatment of pulmonary hypertension</u>”).

* Patients with acute <u>cor pulmonale</u> typically require:

* Stabilization (see “<u>Acute decompensated PH</u>”)

* Intensive management of the underlying cause (see “<u>Treatment of PE</u>”, “<u>Massive PE</u>” and “<u>Treatment of ARDS</u>”).
